cards.front: Recall a key point about Developments in New Materials
cards.back: Smart materials: change properties in response to stimuli — thermochromic (temperature), photochromic (light), shape-memory alloys (heat returns original shape).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Developments in New Materials
cards.back: Nanomaterials: engineered at 1–100 nm scale — graphene (200x stronger than steel, conductive, flexible), carbon nanotubes, nano-coatings.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Developments in New Materials
cards.back: Composites: two or more materials combined for superior properties — carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) for lightweight strength, fibreglass for boat hulls.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Developments in New Materials
cards.back: Hydrogel: water-absorbing polymer — used in contact lenses, wound dressings, agriculture (slow-release water), disposable nappies.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Developments in New Materials
cards.back: Graphene: single layer of carbon atoms — strongest material tested, excellent thermal and electrical conductor, transparent, flexible.

cards.front: What should you know about d&t exam tips?
cards.back: When writing about new materials, use the PPA structure: Properties (what it does), Performance (how it behaves in use), Application (where it is used and why). This demonstrates AO1 + AO2 + AO3 coverage.
SMA (e.g. Shape memory at body temp)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Smart materials and modern materials are the same thing — they are both just new types of plastic. Correct: Smart materials respond to stimuli (temperature, light, stress) by changing properties — e.g. thermochromic pigment changes colour with heat. AQA D&T 8552 assessment: Written exam 50% + NEA 50%. AOs: AO1 Recall (20%), AO2 Apply (30%), AO3 Analyse & evaluate (50%). For grade 9, demonstrate sophisticated understanding of how material properties enable specific design functions and perceptive evaluation of trade-offs.
